1.note: Here, **God of vengeance, Yahweh, God of vengeance** the psalmist is using repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the God who avenges]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **vengeance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who avenges … God who avenges]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually a light that could **shine forth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [Reveal yourself] or [Let them see how majestic you are]

2.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually someone who was sitting or lying down and needed to **rise up**. The psalmist means that God should take action to judge the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Take action] or [Act now]

Here, **the earth** represents all the people who live on the earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [of all people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **recompense**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [pay back] or [punish]

The psalmist is using the adjective **proud** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [proud people]

3.q: עַד־מָתַ֖י רְשָׁעִ֥ים ׀ יְהוָ֑ה עַד־מָ֝תַ֗י רְשָׁעִ֥ים יַעֲלֹֽזוּ
3.note: The psalmist is using the question form **Until when will the wicked, Yahweh, until when will the wicked rejoice** to express his frustration and to make an urgent appeal to God for action. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, the wicked have been rejoicing much too long.]

These two phrases **Until when will the wicked, Yahweh** and **until when will the wicked** are basically the same. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating it again. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. Or if it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, just how long will you allow the wicked to rejoice?]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [wicked people]

4.note: The phrases **pour out** and **speak** express a single idea. The word **pour out** tells more about **speak**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [In large amounts, they speak]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **arrogance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [arrogant words]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [evil actions]

5.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the wicked people were literally **crushing** God’s people with physical force. He means that they are oppressing them severely. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They oppress]

The psalmist is speaking of God’s people as if they were actually **your inheritance**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own people]

6.note: Here, **the widow and the sojourner** and **the fatherless** represent vulnerable people in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [widows and sojourners & they murder those without fathers]

The terms **kill** and **murder** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They kill the widow, the sojourner, and the fatherless]

7.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the wicked people mentioned in the previous verses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The wicked people say]

The implication is that the wicked people are thinking these thoughts silently to themselves rather than speaking them aloud to others. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They say to themselves]

The implication is that God does not see or perceive what the wicked people are doing. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [does not see what we do … does not perceive what we do]

These two phrases **Yah does not see** and **the God of Jacob does not perceive** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh does not see, no, the God of Jacob does not perceive]

8.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You fools need to gain insight!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **insight**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [will you behave insightfully]

8.q: בִּ֭ינוּ בֹּעֲרִ֣ים בָּ⁠עָ֑ם וּ֝⁠כְסִילִ֗ים מָתַ֥י תַּשְׂכִּֽילוּ
8.note: These two phrases **Understand, stupid ones among the people** and **O fools, when will you have insight** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea in a different form. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Get insight and understanding, you stupid, foolish people!]

9.note: Here the psalmist is speaking as if God were actually **planting the ear**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The one creating the ear]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he certainly does hear!]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he certainly does observe!]

10.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [he will certainly rebuke you!]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The one teaching mankind certainly does not lack knowledge.]

Here, **nations** represents the people of all nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [people of all nations]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **knowledge**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Is there anything that the one teaching mankind does not know]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the things that people are thinking]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if people’s thoughts were actually **vapor**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [they are unimportant and useless]

12.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joys**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How joyful is]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the person]

13.note: Here, **to give rest to him** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of God instructing and teaching the blessed person. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [which will allow him to have rest]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe **days** that are characterized by **evil**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [during evil days]

The expression **a pit is dug** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [Yahweh digs a pit]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if God’s punishment of the wicked were actually **a pit** being dug. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh punishes the wicked]

14.q: לֹא־יִטֹּ֣שׁ יְהוָ֣ה עַמּ֑⁠וֹ וְ֝⁠נַחֲלָת֗⁠וֹ לֹ֣א יַעֲזֹֽב
14.note: These two phrases **will not forsake his people** and **he will not abandon his inheritance** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will not forsake his people, no, he will not abandon his inheritance]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if the people of Israel were actually **his inheritance**. He means that they are the people who belong to God in a special way, like a treasured possession that is passed down in a family. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will not abandon Yahweh’s own people]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

15.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [It will happen that]

Here, **judgment** represents “judges” or “the judicial system.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [judges will return to making right judgments]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the right**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being right]

The implication is that all the upright in heart will support and follow righteous judgment when it is restored. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and all the upright in heart are in favor of that]

16.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I cannot find anyone who will rise up for me against the evildoers.]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I cannot find anyone who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness.]

16.q: מִֽי־יָק֣וּם לִ֭⁠י עִם־מְרֵעִ֑ים מִֽי־יִתְיַצֵּ֥ב לִ֝⁠י עִם־פֹּ֥עֲלֵי אָֽוֶן
16.note: These two phrases **Who will rise up for me against the evildoers** and **Who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Who will rise up for me against the evildoers? I say again, who will stand up for me against the workers of wickedness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the people doing wicked things]

17.q: לוּלֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה עֶזְרָ֣תָ⁠ה לִּ֑⁠י כִּ⁠מְעַ֓ט ׀ שָֽׁכְנָ֖ה דוּמָ֣ה נַפְשִֽׁ⁠י
17.note: The psalmist says **Unless Yahweh had been a help to me** to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain what would have happened without God’s help. Use a natural method in your language for introducing an imaginary situation. Alternate translation: [Only because Yahweh was a help to me, my soul did not shortly dwell in silence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **help**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [had helped me]

The psalmist is using one part of a person, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of dying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I]

The psalmist is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **would have dwelt in silence**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [would have been killed]

18.note: By **When I said**, the psalmist means “When I said to myself” or “When I thought to myself.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [When I said to myself]

Here the psalmist is speaking as if his life were actually **a foot that was slipping**. He means that he was in great trouble or danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in big trouble] or [I need help]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Because you are faithful to your covenant, you]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **cares**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [When I am worried about many things]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **consolations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [your console me, which makes my soul glad]
The psalmist is using **my soul** to represent all of himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me]

20.q: הַֽ֭⁠יְחָבְרְ⁠ךָ כִּסֵּ֣א הַוּ֑וֹת יֹצֵ֖ר עָמָ֣ל עֲלֵי־חֹֽק
20.note: The psalmist is using the question form to express that God cannot be allied with corrupt rulers. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You can have nothing to do with a throne of destruction, one who creates injustice by statute.]

Here, **throne** represents a ruler who has authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a ruler who destroys people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a throne that destroys]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [one who creates unjust statutes]

21.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the corrupt rulers from the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Such thrones of destruction conspire together] or [Wicked rulers like that conspire together]

The psalmist is using **against the life of** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to kill” or “to destroy.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill the righteous]

The psalmist is using **innocent blood** as a common expression of his culture to mean “innocent people” or “people who do not deserve to die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they condemn innocent people to death]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **righteous** person. He means righteous people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all righteous people]

22.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **a high tower** because that is a place of protection. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. If not, you could state this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [my protector]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and my God has been the rock]

The psalmist speaks of having God protect him as if God were a place where the psalmist could go to be safe. See how “rock” and “refuge” are translated in Psalms 62:7. Alternate translation: [and my God has kept me safe by his power]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom he worships. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the God whom I worship]

23.note: This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will do the same things to them that they did. Alternate translation: [He will do to them the evil things that they have done to others] or (2) that Yahweh will punish them for their evil. Alternate translation: [He will punish them for the evil things that they have done to others]
The pronoun **them** refers to the corrupt rulers mentioned in verses 20–21. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on those wicked rulers]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sinful things that they have done]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy them their wicked activities]

This could mean: (1) that Yahweh will destroy them because of their wickedness. Alternate translation: [because they have done wicked things] or (2) that Yahweh will destroy them while they are doing wicked things. Alternate translation: [while they are doing wicked things]

These two phrases **he will destroy them in their wickedness** and **Yahweh our God will destroy them** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [and he will destroy them in their wickedness. It is Yahweh our God who will destroy them]
The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean the God whom they worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]
